title: ‘They told us that she is a witch, that’s why we beat her’: 2 Timothy 1:7 and witchcraft accusation-related violence against women in Isuokoma, Nigeria
abstract: This study examines 2 Timothy 1:7 in relation to the growing spate of witchcraft accusation-related violence (WARV) against women in Isuokoma, Nigeria. In Isuokoma, accusations of witchcraft are commonly directed at vulnerable women, particularly the elderly and widows, resulting in social exclusion, physical assault, psychological trauma and sometimes death. Such accusations are, in some cases, sustained by fear-driven narratives embedded within local cosmologies and reinforced in some Pentecostal and/or prophetic movements. Against this backdrop, the study explores how 2 Timothy 1:7, which emphasises that a believer’s life should not be governed by fear but by divine empowerment, can be reread to deconstruct these fear-based cultural and religious narratives that underpin WARV against women in Isuokoma. The study employed a lexical exegetical approach to reread the pericope, alongside in-depth interviews with women who have been accused of witchcraft, their family members and church leaders in Isuokoma. A purposive sampling technique guided the selection of nine participants, and the data were analysed qualitatively and presented thematically in the study. The study argued that a contextual rereading of 2 Timothy 1:7 can help to challenge narratives that sacralise fear and suspicion, and also foster a community characterised by spiritual courage, love and sound judgement. As part of the recommendations, the study highlights implications for safeguarding and pastoral practice, including trauma-informed care, community education, and other strategies aimed at enhancing the protection, psychosocial well-being, dignity and safety of women accused of witchcraft in Isuokoma. Contribution: This ethnographic study offers a theological framework and practical recommendations for challenging fear-driven narratives and supporting women who are often the victims of witchcraft accusations.

title: World Englishes in the 21st century: new perspectives and challenges to the dynamic model
Workplace health interventions in SMEs – experiences of employees performing as in-house facilitators
journal: International Journal of Workplace Health Management
abstract: Purpose Facilitation is a key factor in workplace health and organizational interventions. However, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) often lack the resources needed to access professional facilitation. The purpose of this study is to examine how in-house facilitators are experienced in workplace health interventions in SMEs and to identify the qualities that enable in-house facilitators to perform this facilitation role effectively as an alternative to engaging external facilitators or internal professional process consultants. Design/methodology/approach A multiple-case study approach was used across three Danish SMEs in the manufacturing and Information Technology sectors, each of which conducted two interventions. Each company appointed two in-house facilitators among employees who had no formal facilitator training. Data were collected over six months through FishBone, Chronological Workshops and interviews with employees, in-house facilitators and managers, followed by a completion survey. Findings The in-house facilitators supported the identification of workplace health issues and contributed with contextually relevant solutions. Besides demonstrating established facilitator competencies, participants highlighted two key characteristics: (1) contextual sensitivity; the ability to align actions with the organizational environment and participant needs and (2) creative problem-solving based on personal experience and interest, akin to the role of a bricoleur, reflecting agency and adaptability. These qualities positioned in-house facilitators as a viable, context-sensitive alternative to external consultants. Originality/value By leveraging employees' insider knowledge, relational trust and informal competencies, SMEs can strengthen organizational interventions and enhance employee well-being. The findings suggest that SMEs may hold untapped resources within their workplace to drive successful interventions.

title: Working-memory load and task-dependent functional connectivity in competitive football players and novice controls: an exploratory fMRI study
journal: BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation
abstract: Abstract This exploratory fMRI study examined whether football expertise is associated with load-dependent differences in domain-general working-memory processing. Forty university students (20 competitive football players and 20 sex-matched novice controls) completed a 12-block numerical 0-, 1-, and 2-back task. Increasing load reduced overall accuracy and increased correct-target reaction time and inverse efficiency scores, whereas no statistically significant group main effects or group-by-load interactions were detected. Corrected whole-brain activation and activation-space analyses likewise showed no between-group differences. Generalized psychophysiological interaction analysis using Brainnetome-defined left A39rv/PGa and right dIa seeds identified two novices > football players effects for the 2-back − 0-back contrast after whole-brain FDR correction in DPABI (corrected p < .05, cluster extent k > 30 voxels). These effects involved A39rv/PGa coupling with a midline/caudate-adjacent region and dIa coupling with the right inferior occipital gyrus. Condition-specific estimates indicated divergent load-related trajectories rather than simply stronger coupling in novices during 2-back. The findings suggest expertise-related differences in load-dependent network modulation but do not establish behavioral equivalence or neural efficiency. Independent replication is required.

title: When the internet cools crops: the mitigating effect of digital infrastructure on heat-induced grain losses in China
abstract: High temperatures are increasingly threatening the stability of grain output and food security in the context of climate change. Yet there is currently a lack of empirical evidence to show whether the development of digital infrastructure can help mitigate the adverse effects of high temperatures on grain output. Using data from 294 prefecture-level cities in China over the period 2010–2023, we estimated the effect of high-temperature risks and digital infrastructure on grain output. We also examined whether digital infrastructure moderates the relationship between high-temperature disasters and grain output. We find that high-temperature risks significantly suppressed grain output; there is an inverted U-shaped relationship between digital infrastructure construction and grain output; digital infrastructure can mitigate the loss of grain output caused by high-temperature risks, and its buffering effect is mainly concentrated in the central and western regions as well as regions with lower exposure to high temperatures. Improving agricultural information acquisition, optimizing the allocation of production factors, enhancing digital risk sharing and financial security, and accelerating the adoption of climate-adaptive technologies are important mechanisms for the functioning of agricultural digital resilience. This paper incorporates digital infrastructure construction into the agricultural climate adaptation framework, clarifies the conditions for the effective functioning of agricultural digital resilience, and provides insights for the development of digital infrastructure in grain-producing regions exposed to high-temperature risks.

title: When schools close: Crisis governance and education continuity in Thailand’s border conflict
journal: Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences Studies
abstract: The 2025 Thai-Cambodian border conflict closed roughly 751 schools and displaced over 131,000 students across four northeastern Thai provinces, exposing how a functioning, non-fragile state can nonetheless govern a crisis with no plan at all. Drawing on crisis governance and policy process theory, this study asks why a foreseeable risk never produced a pre-conflict continuity policy, and what happened to decision-making once the conflict removed that option. Using a qualitative design, the study analyzes 28 semi-structured interviews and open-ended questionnaires with education administrators, supervisors, school leaders, teachers, and parents across the affected provinces, supplemented by four interviews with local administrative organization officers probing the fiscal-governance dimension of the resulting framework. Three findings emerge: the absence of a national education-continuity policy left front-line administrators and teachers as de facto policymakers, improvising under the conditions of street-level bureaucracy; the conflict functioned as a focusing event that could have opened a policy window, but has not yet been converted into legislation; and psychosocial and staffing gaps were compounded because no institution held clear coordinating authority. Building on these findings, the study develops the SHIELD Model (Structural, Hybrid, Interagency, Emotional, Leadership, and Data-driven framework), a six-component crisis-governance architecture that operationalizes the sense-making, coordinating, and learning tasks central to crisis leadership theory at the national, service-area, and school levels. The Model offers a template for converting a focusing event into durable continuity policy before, rather than after, the next crisis.

title: When participation is not inclusion: the service-participation paradox in mental health
abstract: Purpose This conceptual paper aims to examine why increased participation in mental health services does not necessarily produce social inclusion and develops a framework for distinguishing participation that expands a person’s social world from participation that remains contained within services. Design/methodology/approach As a conceptual paper, it develops a theoretical distinction and framework by drawing on selected literature on mental health recovery, social inclusion, community integration and occupational engagement. Findings The paper introduces the service-participation paradox, whereby services can successfully increase participation while leaving a person’s wider social world largely unchanged. It distinguishes service-contained from inclusion-oriented participation, proposes a two-dimensional matrix crossing participation intensity with social-world expansion and offers a sustainability heuristic for examining what remains beyond the service’s direct organisation and mediation, alongside meaning, choice and agency as person-centred criteria for interpreting both dimensions. Practical implications Services are encouraged to evaluate participation not only by attendance but by whether it is meaningful, chosen and expands access to relationships, roles and settings beyond the service system. Originality/value The paper offers a novel conceptual framing of the relationship between service-organised participation and social inclusion, bringing together the service-participation paradox, a distinction between service-contained and inclusion-oriented participation and heuristic tools for examining social-world expansion.

title: Values, risk perceptions and pro-environmental behaviour among university students: evidence from Indonesian higher education
journal: Journal of Applied Research in Higher Education
abstract: Purpose This study examined value-based, risk-cognitive and normative antecedents of pro-environmental behaviour (PEB) among Indonesian university students by integrating value–belief–norm theory, protection motivation theory and the theory of planned behaviour. Design/methodology/approach A cross-sectional survey of 614 undergraduates from 16 Indonesian universities was analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM), with predictive validity assessed through the cross-validated predictive ability test (CVPAT). Findings Of the 16 direct paths tested, 11 were significant. Pro-environmental intention predicted PEB with a large effect, which was strongest in the model. Injunctive norms and perceived behavioural control were the leading predictors of intention. Altruistic values predicted attitude and biospheric values predicted intention directly. Both anthropocentric and ecocentric risk perceptions significantly predicted attitudes and intentions. Descriptive norms and egoistic values were not significant. Practical implications Indonesian higher education institutions should prioritise intention formation over awareness-only approaches, strengthen injunctive normative climates through institutional leadership and invest in enabling campus infrastructure, consistent with the Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) for 2030 roadmap and Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 4 and 13. Originality/value This study is among the first to integrate tripartite value orientations, dual-dimension risk perceptions and differentiated social norms in a single PLS-SEM model of student PEB in Indonesian higher education, an underrepresented context in sustainability in higher education research.

title: Resistance to mall expansion: still not buying the destination argument
journal: Journal of Place Management and Development
abstract: Purpose The purpose of this study is to analyse stakeholders’ reactions to expansion arguments for an out-of-town shopping mall in a contested planning process. The proposed expansion occurs against a backdrop of growing competition from e-commerce and increasing pressure on physical retail formats. This study seeks to explain how these arguments function as a means of making expansion appear feasible and desirable for place development, and whether they remain persuasive despite critique and uncertainty. Design/methodology/approach This study is based on a document analysis of 144 formal stakeholder considerations submitted in response to the expansion vision of a Swedish shopping mall, examining how stakeholders engage with and contest expansion arguments. Findings This study identifies a destination argument that legitimises mall expansion through claims of uniqueness, experiencification and an expanded hinterland. Stakeholders frequently contest these claims, not because they lack information, but because they hold competing views on retail place development and its consequences. The findings show how destination arguments can remain influential despite substantial scepticism and critique. Practical implications The findings suggest greater scrutiny of destination arguments used to justify mall expansion. Claims of uniqueness, wider catchment areas and spillover benefits should be assessed against redistribution effects and alternative development paths. As e-commerce and mall experiencification intensify competition, city-centre actors may need stronger collaboration and clearer articulation of city-centre values. Originality/value This study introduces the concept of the destination argument as a legitimising strategy in mall expansion and shifts attention from stakeholder positions and impacts to the interactive processes through which expansion gains legitimacy in contested planning environments.
